title: K-th Smallest Prime Fraction
description: Brute force to optimized: generating and sorting all fractions versus binary searching the fraction value with an O(n) two-pointer count.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a sorted array arr of distinct positive integers (representing a set of primes, though the algorithm works for any sorted positive values) and an integer k, consider every fraction arr[i]/arr[j] where 0 <= i < j < arr.length. Return the k-th smallest such fraction as an array [numerator, denominator].

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"k-th smallest value among a huge implicit set of pairs\"","Binary search on the answer VALUE, counting how many pairs are <= a candidate at each step"],["All fractions are between 0 and 1 (since arr[i] < arr[j] for i<j)","A natural binary search range of [0, 1] for the fraction value"]]}

blocks.text: Since arr is sorted and i < j is required, every fraction arr[i]/arr[j] is strictly less than 1. As a candidate threshold x increases from 0 to 1, the COUNT of fractions arr[i]/arr[j] that are <= x increases monotonically, which is exactly the condition needed to binary search directly on x rather than generating all fractions.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the k-th Cheapest Price Ratio Among Many Product Pairs
blocks.text: Picture many products with known prices, and considering every possible ratio of a cheaper product's price to a pricier one's. Instead of computing every ratio and sorting them (which could be a huge list), you can binary search directly on a candidate ratio value and count how many pairs fall below it, homing in on the exact k-th one.

blocks.caption: The count of fractions below a threshold x grows monotonically as x increases, enabling binary search on x itself

blocks.text: Result: [2, 5]. The fractions in sorted order are 1/5, 1/3, 2/5, 1/2, 3/5, 2/3, and the 3rd smallest is 2/5.

Before generating all O(n squared) fractions and sorting them, notice that binary searching directly on the fraction VALUE, and counting how many arr[i]/arr[j] pairs fall below a candidate threshold using a two-pointer sweep (since arr is sorted), finds the k-th smallest fraction without ever materializing the full list.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For a fixed numerator index i, as the candidate threshold x increases, more denominator indices j satisfy arr[i]/arr[j] <= x, specifically all j from some point onward (since arr is sorted ascending, larger arr[j] means a smaller fraction).

Observation 2: This means for each i, a two-pointer approach (a single pointer j that only moves forward as i increases) can count, in amortized O(1) per i, how many valid j indices satisfy arr[i] <= x*arr[j].

Observation 3: Summing this count across all i gives the TOTAL number of fractions <= x, in O(n) total for a fixed x, which lets a binary search over x locate the threshold where this count first reaches exactly k.

Observation 4: While counting, tracking the LARGEST fraction encountered that is still <= x directly gives the actual k-th smallest fraction once the count matches k exactly, avoiding a separate reconstruction step.

This leads to binary searching over the fraction value x in [0, 1], using a two-pointer sweep to count fractions <= x in O(n) per check, and tracking the largest such fraction to directly report the answer once the count equals k.
Generate every fraction arr[i]/arr[j] for i < j, sort them all, and return the k-th smallest.

items: For every pair i < j, compute the fraction arr[i]/arr[j] (or keep it as a pair to avoid floating-point comparison issues).
Sort all these fractions by value.
Return the k-th smallest (index k-1) from this sorted list.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Generating and sorting all fractions directly implements the definition, and is straightforward to verify.
It costs O(n squared log n) for n up to 1000 (about half a million fractions), noticeably slower than the binary search approach.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared log n), generating O(n squared) fractions and sorting them.
Space: O(n squared) to store all fractions.

Limitation: materializing every fraction is unnecessary; binary searching directly on the fraction value, counting via a two-pointer sweep, finds the answer in O(n log(max value)) without ever storing all pairs.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why generating all fractions is wasteful: the actual goal is just to identify ONE specific fraction (the k-th smallest), not to have the full sorted list available.

The binary-search-on-value trick: since the count of fractions <= x is a monotonically non-decreasing function of x, binary search can directly narrow in on the threshold value where this count first reaches k.

Counting efficiently for a fixed x: for each numerator index i (from left to right), the smallest valid denominator index j satisfying arr[i] <= x*arr[j] only moves FORWARD as i increases (since arr is sorted), enabling an O(n) two-pointer sweep per count check instead of a nested loop.

Recovering the actual answer: while performing the count for the current candidate x, tracking the LARGEST fraction found that is still <= x directly gives the actual k-th smallest fraction once the count exactly equals k, avoiding any separate reconstruction pass.

Binary search x in [0, 1]. For each candidate x, use a two-pointer sweep over i and j to count fractions arr[i]/arr[j] <= x in O(n), tracking the largest such fraction. Narrow the search range based on whether the count is below, above, or exactly k.

blocks.caption: Binary search on the fraction value, counting via a two-pointer sweep, tracking the largest qualifying fraction

blocks.text: Because arr is sorted, for a fixed candidate x, as i increases the required denominator index j (the smallest j satisfying arr[i] <= x*arr[j]) only moves forward, never backward, allowing a single two-pointer pass to count all qualifying pairs in O(n) total rather than O(n squared). Since the count of fractions <= x is monotonic in x, binary search correctly converges on the threshold where the count exactly equals k; the largest fraction tracked during that final count check is, by construction, exactly the k-th smallest fraction overall.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log(precision needed)), each binary search iteration costs O(n) via the two-pointer count.
Space: O(1) extra.

blocks.text: K-th Smallest Prime Fraction is a strong example of "binary search on the answer" combined with an O(n) two-pointer counting subroutine, avoiding the need to ever materialize the full set of candidate values.

items: Resetting the two-pointer j back to 1 for every i within a single count pass, which would make each count check O(n squared) instead of O(n).
Comparing arr[i]/arr[j] using floating-point division for the "largest fraction" tracking instead of cross-multiplication, risking precision errors.

blocks.text: Explicitly naming this as "binary search on the answer, with an O(n) counting subroutine enabled by the sorted input" ties it clearly to a broader, reusable technique family.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "k-th smallest value among an implicit, huge set of pairs", think: binary search on the value itself, count qualifying pairs with a two-pointer sweep.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n squared log n) time and O(n squared) space; the binary search approach runs in O(n log(precision)) time and O(1) space, directly exploiting the sorted input and monotonic count.

items: Pattern: binary search on the answer value, combined with an O(n) two-pointer counting subroutine.
Core Idea: binary search the fraction value x; count fractions <= x via a two-pointer sweep (j never resets); track the largest qualifying fraction to directly report the answer.
Time: O(n squared log n) for the brute force, O(n log(precision)) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: the count of pairs below a threshold is monotonic, and a sorted array enables an O(n) (not O(n squared)) two-pointer count per threshold check.
Interview Difficulty: a strong, non-obvious application of binary search on the answer combined with two pointers.
One line memory trick: binary search the fraction value; count with a two-pointer sweep; track the largest qualifying fraction.
